raze

/RAYZ/ - sounds exactly like raise · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Raze means to tear a structure down completely to the ground.

Wrecking crews razed the empty cannery in nine days, and by spring only a gravel pad marked the block.

Example

When the Great Fire of 1666 outran London's bucket lines, the king's men stopped fighting the flames and started starving them: with fire-hooks and axes they razed whole streets of untouched houses ahead of the blaze, pulling roofs and timbers flat so the fire would arrive and find nothing standing to feed on. Householders wept, and helped. The gaps worked where the water had not.

Raze is the exact word for that tactic, because it means to tear a structure down completely to the ground — the phrase razed to the ground is nearly one word in English. Demolish shares the work but not the emphasis; you can demolish a wall and keep the house. Raze insists on level: when the crews finish, the site reads as ground, not as building.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

demolish: Demolish is the engineer's everyday word for tearing built things down on purpose, and it is satisfied by the act at any size — you can demolish one wall and keep the house. Raze accepts nothing partial: a razed site reads as ground, nothing left standing.

level: To level a building is to bring it flat with the ground, and the word stays as calm as a surveyor's tool. Raze means the same flattening with the violence left showing — fire-hooks, wrecking balls, a structure deliberately brought to nothing — which is why headlines reach for it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

erect: to put a structure up

rebuild: to put it back up after loss

Where it sits · how completely the building comes down

damage → gut → raze

damage vs. raze: Damage is the loosest rung — anything from a cracked pane to a burnt wing, with the building still a building — while raze ends the scale with the whole structure brought down to the ground.

gut vs. raze: Gut goes further than damage — the whole interior is destroyed even while the shell stands — but raze claims the most: nothing left upright at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — raze: to scrape (Latin radere, via French raser)

Put it together: There is no prefix or suffix to peel: raze is Latin radere, "to scrape," worn smooth by French raser on its way into English. The scraping is the meaning — a razed block has been scraped off the earth's surface the way a razor scrapes a jaw — and razor is the same root naming the same motion.

Use the root in a new word: razor: The barber drew the straight razor along the jaw in long, unhurried passes.

Root Check

Word Choice

stark / journalistic

Raze is a whole-structure verb: buildings, blocks, fortresses brought level with the ground — headline writers love its four ruthless letters. Demolish is the engineer's everyday word; level, the plain one. In this unit's division of labor, pillage empties a place and leaves it standing; raze leaves nothing standing; obliterate erases even the trace that it stood.
